description:
Hi! I’m Amna, a high school graduate taking a gap year to teach myself engineering. I build electronics, robotics, embedded systems and software projects, documenting my journey on YouTube (halfbuiltbyamna).

For NASA Space Apps, I’m forming Tesseract to build a Space Mission Design Game. Looking for teammates interested in game dev, programming, UI/UX, space science, physics, AI/ML, 3D design or storytelling.
summary: Among Orbits is a free, browser-playable, retro pixel-art multiplayer game that teaches space mission design through hands-on engineering trade-offs. One to four players walk around a mission control facility and design a small satellite mission together at four stations: Propulsion & Launch (rocket and orbit), Payload Bay (science instruments), Power & Systems Core (solar arrays and batteries) and Comms Deck (radio band and link budget). Every choice affects the others: instruments add mass, power draw and data; batteries add mass; stronger radios draw more power. When the crew launches, the game flies the design through a 3-day mission under real space weather pulled live from NASA's DONKI API, where geomagnetic storms drain batteries faster and solar flares black out radios. Instead of a generic "Game Over", players get an Engineering Failure Report that explains the root cause with real numbers and how to fix it. Students and newcomers experience how spacecraft subsystems interact as one system, learn by iterating, and practise the teamwork real mission teams rely on.
details:
What it does and how it works

Among Orbits is a 2D pixel-art cooperative mission design game, playable in any web browser at https://nasa-space-apps-tessaract.vercel.app/. Players start solo and walks around a facility with a central hub and four station rooms. We also have a version of this game in Unity which is Multiplayer where Players can host a room and share a 6-character code so up to four friends can join from their own browsers. Each crewmate picks a color and a role (Flight Director, Systems Engineer, Payload Specialist, Comms & Telemetry Officer).

Propulsion & Launch: choose a launch vehicle and target orbit (LEO, SSO, GTO, Deep Space); the game checks spacecraft mass against the rocket's payload capacity for that orbit.

Payload Bay: choose science instruments; their mass, power draw and data rate are totalled, and spacecraft dry mass is estimated from the payload's share of a small spacecraft's mass.

Power & Systems Core: pick deployable or body-mounted solar panels and size the array and battery. The array must power the load and recharge the battery in sunlight; the battery must last through the eclipse. Extra power-system mass makes the spacecraft heavier.

Comms Deck: pick a radio band (UHF, S, X, Ka) and transmit power. A link budget (free-space path loss, signal-to-noise, data rate capped by radio hardware) decides whether the science data reaches the ground each day. A stronger transmitter draws more power.

LAUNCH SIMULATION plays a launch cinematic, the battery charges in sunlight and drains in eclipse, storms drain it faster, radiation degrades the solar arrays, and the downlink is measured against the data generated. The first failure stops the mission. For example: "Battery depleted during eclipse. 32.4 W load emptied the 10 Wh battery in 18.5 min of a 36 min eclipse."

NASA data

The game polls NASA's DONKI API every 30 seconds for geomagnetic storms, solar flares, coronal mass ejections, solar energetic particle events and high-speed streams. It turns them into gameplay effects: storms drain batteries faster, M-class flares halve the radio link, X-class flares black it out, particle events degrade solar arrays, and high-speed streams raise attitude-control power. The same design can succeed on a calm day and fail during a storm. A live ticker shows current conditions, and an Offline Drill mode uses a preset storm when the API is unreachable. Launch vehicle capacities are derived from NASA Launch Services Program performance data. Solar, battery, mass-ratio and instrument benchmarks are adapted from NASA's State-of-the-Art Small Spacecraft Technology report.

Benefits and intended impact

Mission design is usually taught with spreadsheets and theory, and each subsystem in isolation. Among Orbits makes the system-level trade-offs tangible: players see that adding a radar instrument overloads the downlink, or that a minimal battery fails once real storm conditions hit. Failure becomes a learning tool, because the report tells players why the mission failed and what to change. It runs free in a browser with nothing to install, so classrooms, clubs and self-learners can use it anywhere.

Tools and technologies

Space Agency Partner and Other Data

- NASA Open APIs (DONKI API access): https://api.nasa.gov
- NASA State-of-the-Art Small Spacecraft Technology report: https://www.nasa.gov/smallsat-institute/sst-soa/
- NASA Launch Services Program: https://www.nasa.gov/kennedy/launch-services-program/
-NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information): https://kauai.ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/DONKI/

Creativity

We combined a social-deduction-style walkable crew game with a real engineering simulator, so designing a spacecraft feels like moving through a crewed facility rather than filling in a form. Live space weather means no two days play the same, and a pixel-art launch cinematic turns every test flight into an event. Engineering failure reports replace "Game Over" screens, so failing is part of learning.

Scientific honesty: values come from the mission configuration built on NASA data. Where we simplified (eclipse durations, ground contact time, required signal margin, implementation losses, amplifier efficiency), the game labels it a simplified model.
Accessibility: it runs in a browser, works solo, and has clear on-screen guidance.
Resilience: it keeps working offline with a storm preset if the NASA API can't be reached.

Team: Amna Fatima, Taha Saddique, Kaynat Naqvi, Ahmad Salman
